## The Physics of Evacuation in a Blocked System

Vacuuming an A/C system from the low side alone is mechanically feasible but technically insufficient for a system where the high-side Schrader valve is inaccessible and the line is discontinued. In your 1990 Suburban, if you cannot remove the service port cap or install a new manifold gauge with a built-in valve on the high side, you are left with a single access point. While this allows the pump to pull air out of the low-pressure side (the evaporator and accumulator), it leaves the condenser, compressor head, and the disconnected high-side line completely isolated from the vacuum.

The fundamental principle here is fluid dynamics and pressure equalization. When you connect your vacuum pump to the low-side service port and crank the engine over with the A/C clutch engaged, the compressor acts as a blower, pulling air through the system toward the suction line. However, once that air passes the piston in the compressor cylinder, it moves into the discharge side. If there is no way for that air to exit the high-pressure circuit (because your Schrader valve is welded shut or missing), the vacuum will stall at a specific threshold determined by the volume of the high-side component versus the low-side component.

You might observe the gauge dropping quickly in the first few minutes, creating an illusion of success. But as soon as the pump has evacuated all the air from the low side and the compressor chambers, it encounters the "dead head" of the disconnected high side. The pressure will equilibrate at a level significantly above zero absolute pressure—often hovering around 1 to 3 inches of mercury depending on the size of the condenser relative to the evaporator. This is not an adequate vacuum for removing moisture or non-condensables, which require pressures typically below 500 microns (roughly 0.5 inHg) to ensure water vapor condenses and is pulled out as liquid rather than remaining as gas.

## The Role of the High-Pressure Circuit

In a standard evacuation procedure, you utilize both service ports to create a continuous path from the vacuum source through the entire closed loop. By blocking the high side, you effectively split the system into two separate volumes connected only by the compressor's moving parts. The pump struggles against the larger volume of the condenser and discharge line without an outlet valve on that end.

If you proceed with low-side-only evacuation in this specific scenario, you risk leaving significant amounts of moisture trapped inside the condenser or the high-pressure hose. Moisture is the enemy of A/C systems because it turns to ice during operation, blocking refrigerant flow (ice plugs), and reacts with oil to form acidic sludge that destroys compressor bearings. Since your Napa order for a new hose without a valve confirms that the physical barrier on the high side cannot be easily bypassed during the initial pull-down, the system will never reach the deep vacuum required for effective drying.

## Alternative Strategies for Inaccessible Valves

When faced with a discontinued line or a non-removable Schrader valve, the industry standard workaround is to drill out the existing core of the blocked valve and install a new service port directly into the copper tubing using a flare tool kit designed for this purpose. This requires cutting the old line slightly longer than the original specification if space permits, but it restores full access to both sides of the system.

If drilling is not an option due to structural constraints or safety concerns, you can attempt a "wet evacuation" technique, though this carries risks. This involves pressurizing the high side with refrigerant (if available) before evacuating from the low side, theoretically forcing air out through the compressor discharge. However, this method is largely obsolete and unreliable for removing moisture compared to a true deep vacuum. It also introduces the risk of over-pressurizing an old system with compromised seals.

The most reliable path forward for your 1990 Suburban, given the missing valve, is to have Napa fabricate a hose assembly that includes a Schrader adapter or a bulkhead fitting specifically designed to screw into the discontinuous line end, effectively creating a new high-side port. Once installed, you can then proceed with standard two-point evacuation protocols. Without this restoration of access, the system remains compromised, and any future A/C performance issues will likely trace back to residual moisture in the condenser that was never properly evacuated.
